data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The reliability gain is genuine rather than mere compliance if and only if the panel's item-level judgments predict outcomes independently of the checklist's global answer key, and the panel shows transfer to reordered or rephrased checklists that the panelists have not seen.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist is so detailed that it functions as a complete decision tree, independent item-level signal is unnecessary\u2014the checklist itself is the expertise, and mere compliance is sufficient for reliability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If reordering the checklist introduces confusion that degrades performance even for understanding panelists (e.g., because earlier items provide context for later items), the transfer test is invalid.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task is so simple that both understanding and compliance yield ceiling-level accuracy, the transfer test cannot distinguish them.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Mere checklist compliance that tracks the right answer means panelists are following the checklist's algorithm mechanically without understanding the items. In that case, their item-level responses are fully explained by the checklist's content and yield no independent predictive power. Genuine reliability gain requires that panelists have learned, through training, to recognize the features the checklist points to\u2014so their responses carry signal beyond the checklist structure. Transfer to reordered or rephrased checklists is a direct test: if panelists rely on understanding rather than positional compliance, reordering items should not degrade their accuracy; if they rely on rote sequence, it will.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
